Investment memo · MAERSK.B-DK · 8 November 2026

A.P. Møller - Mærsk (MAERSK.B-DK): a well-run survivor at the top of a disruption-driven earnings peak, with earnings about to turn down and the better entry point a year or more away

The recommendation for Richard, in four points

  1. Do not own Maersk at DKK 22,870. The share price already discounts the upside scenario: my base-case total return is about -25% over eighteen months, and the scenario-weighted return is about -20%.
  2. Fair value is DKK 14,000-17,000 (central DKK 15,500, about 0.55x book). Three independent methods (through-cycle earnings, book value and the sum of the parts) land in the same range.
  3. The pivot is Maersk's first FY2027 guidance in early February 2027. I expect a range of roughly 6-9bn of EBITDA, below the 9.3bn consensus, with no new buyback more likely than not.
  4. Prepare to buy the 2027-2028 trough. At 0.4-0.5x book, with scrapping starting and ship deliveries falling from 2029, Maersk becomes a quality-cyclical trough-on-trough setup; a re-rating from 0.45x to 0.8x book would return 75-80% plus dividends.

Money in USD unless stated; share prices in DKK. Every return is measured from DKK 22,870 (23 October 2026). The price basis, the forecast sources, the inputs I changed, a glossary and the reconciliation of figures that differ between sources are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: the key insights, implications and conclusions

1

Maersk's earnings depend on one variable, the Ocean freight rate, and that variable is about to turn down. Group earnings equal Maersk's average loaded Ocean freight rate multiplied by about 13.6m FFE (forty-foot equivalent units) a year, less a cost per container that is nearly fixed for each sailing. On Maersk's own sensitivity, rebuilt from its disclosures, a USD 100 per FFE change in the annual average rate moves EBITDA and EBIT by about 1.36bn and EPS by about USD 95; EPS moves almost one for one because Ocean profit is taxed under the tonnage-tax regime and so carries almost no marginal tax. Every other driver is small by comparison: 100k FFE of volume moves EBIT by about 10m, and a USD 100 a tonne move in bunker fuel costs 0.2-0.3bn net of surcharge recovery. Beneath the rate sits an earnings floor of 2.3-2.9bn of EBIT from Terminals and Logistics & Services, and that floor is the only part of the group the market should value on earnings.

2

The 2026 earnings peak is a disruption peak, and the Q3 2026 results showed what the disruption costs Maersk. In Q3 2026 Maersk's loaded freight rate reached USD 3,287 per FFE (+46% year on year), underlying EBITDA reached 4.71bn, and management raised FY2026 guidance for the third time in five months, to 14.0-14.5bn of EBITDA (from 10.5-12.5bn in August and 4.5-7.0bn in February). Yet Q3 EBITDA missed consensus by about 14% and EBIT missed by about 11% (3.3bn against 3.7bn), because loaded volume fell 1% and Ocean unit cost at constant fuel prices rose 5%.

The bulls' landside-bottleneck thesis misses this cost. The port congestion that props up freight rates also raises Maersk's operating costs, caps its volume (vessel utilisation is 96%, which leaves nothing more to sell) and broke the schedule reliability of Gemini, Maersk's network partnership with Hapag-Lloyd (68% in August-September against 90% before). Earnings supported by congestion are therefore of lower quality than earnings supported by freight rates alone.

3

From 2027, the most visible supply wave in the industry's history meets the unwinding of its largest temporary capacity buffer. Fleet capacity grows 7.4% in 2027 and 13.2% in 2028 on Bernstein's count (9.5% and 12.7% on Clarksons'), against demand growth of 2-4%. The orderbook equals 42-44% of the fleet, scrapping is near zero (41k TEU, twenty-foot equivalent units, in 2026), idle capacity is only 2.2%, and the industry's net cash of 26-30bn lets carriers play a "game of chicken" rather than cut capacity. Meanwhile the buffer is unwinding: Suez Canal transits are back to 59% of pre-crisis levels and rising, a full return releases about 7% of effective capacity, and the Suez Canal Authority expects all Maersk services back on the route by March 2027.

I put the probability that freight rates fall in 2027 above 85%. The level of rates, however, is unforecastable to within a factor of three: FY2027 EBITDA plausibly spans 3.7bn (a 2016-type price war coinciding with a fast Suez return) to 14.5bn (a renewed closure of the Red Sea or the Strait of Hormuz).

4

My forecasts sit below consensus in every year from FY2027, and the gap is widest below EBIT, where the sell-side's analysis is thinnest. My FY2027 EBITDA of 8.4bn compares with a post-Q3 Bloomberg consensus of about 9.3bn (FactSet's consensus was 8.7bn before the Q3 results). My FY2028 EBITDA of 6.3bn compares with consensus of 7.5bn, and my FY2029 EBITDA of 7.15bn with two brokers' 8.6bn. At EPS the gap is much wider (USD 112, -46 and -15 against 125, 62 and 119), because three items that the sell-side does not model reverse together at the trough:

  • A tax charge of 0.4-0.5bn a year that does not fall with profit, because Ocean losses earn no tax relief while Terminals and Logistics profits are taxed.
  • Interest income that decays as 15bn of net cash is spent on capex, leases and the FY2026 dividend.
  • The end of the 1bn-a-year share buyback.

Together these three items are worth about USD 60 a share in FY2028. Consensus FY2028 EBIT of 0.8bn consists almost entirely of the 0.7bn annual depreciation benefit from Maersk's extension of its vessels' useful lives, so in economic terms consensus already places the trough at break-even. Only DNB Carnegie has written down what break-even EBIT means for EPS.

5

The share price discounts the upside scenario, not the base case. Every valuation and sentiment reading sits at an extreme:

  • the shares trade at about 0.8x FY2026 book value, against 0.4-0.5x at the 2016 and 2023 troughs and 0.6x as recently as August 2026;
  • the two-year-forward P/E is 92x, the 100th percentile of its ten-year range (median 15x; 90th percentile 22x);
  • relative strength is in the 97th percentile after an 80% share price rise in twelve months;
  • only 8% of analysts rate the shares Buy, and the mean target price is 13% below the share price.

My fair value is DKK 14,000-17,000 (central DKK 15,500, about 0.55x book), the same answer as a sum of the parts that values Ocean at nil. From DKK 22,870 that fair value gives a base-case total return of about -25% over eighteen months and about -13% over three years, including a FY2026 dividend of about DKK 1,300. Weighting the three scenarios (50% base, 30% deeper downturn, 20% disruption-extended) gives an eighteen-month return of about -20%.

6

The skew that matters for Richard is negative, because the share price already sits where the upside scenario would put it. On fundamentals the range of outcomes is two-sided. The downside is more probable, because the orderbook is contractual; the upside is larger and faster, because a Hormuz or Red Sea event re-absorbs capacity within weeks. On price, the skew is one-sided. Maersk today is the mirror image of a trough-on-trough setup: peak earnings, a peak multiple percentile and peak momentum, with the earnings turn one to two quarters ahead.

The opportunity in Maersk is real but dated. The 2027-2028 trough, at 0.4-0.5x book, with scrapping starting and deliveries falling from 2029, is a quality-cyclical trough-on-trough setup worth preparing for. That setup has not arrived yet.

7

Four developments would prove me wrong; in order of probability, they are:

  1. a renewed Red Sea closure or Hormuz escalation (about 20%);
  2. the Asia-Europe contract season settling near 2026 levels (carriers are asking for increases, and COSCO expects its 2027 contract rates to rise year on year), which would hold H1 2027 rates up and delay the reset by two quarters without cancelling it;
  3. a 2bn buyback in February 2027 (Morgan Stanley expects one; I put the probability of some buyback programme at about 45%);
  4. management's landside-constraint thesis proving right, which Drewry's data argue against: port utilisation outside China is 60-70%, and 58m TEU of terminal capacity is being added in 2026.

The five judgements that move the shares, with their arithmetic, follow topic #12.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

The 2026 tailwind is temporary capacity absorption that is already fading, while the 2027-2028 headwind is a contracted supply wave; the operating environment is therefore already net negative on any horizon beyond the current quarter.

The tailwind is capacity absorption, not demand. In 2026, rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope absorbs about 7% of the fleet, and port congestion absorbs a further 8.5-12.6%: 4.3m TEU sat in queues in Q3 after the China typhoon season, and waiting times at Shanghai reached twelve days. Global container volumes grew about 5% in H1 2026, but that growth included tariff front-loading.

The headwind is contracted supply. Deliveries of new ships total 3.29m TEU in 2027 and 5.23m TEU in 2028 on Jefferies' count. A cash-rich industry has kept ordering through every oversupply warning: the orderbook grew by about 1.6m TEU in Q3 2026 alone, and Maersk itself ordered about 500k TEU for delivery in 2029-2030. Scrapping is near zero.

Demand is a minor partner. The ratio of trade growth to GDP growth has fallen from about 2x before 2008 to 1-1.2x. The average US tariff is 22.8%, consumer confidence is weak (the University of Michigan index stands at 46.3), and Morgan Stanley expects an air pocket in volumes in late 2026 after the front-loading.

Input costs are a headwind that Maersk currently recovers from customers. Brent crude was USD 111 a barrel in late October. The EU Emissions Trading System will cover 100% of verified emissions, at a cost of about 0.5bn a year by 2027. Vessel charters are locked in until 2031 at about USD 41,000 a day, and 9.3bn of leases are committed but not yet started.

Management's landside-bottleneck thesis fails outside China. Management's case for structurally higher freight rates is that terminal capacity grew 21% from 2019 while trade grew 28%. The regional data show that the terminal shortage is Chinese and weather-driven, not global. Greater China terminal utilisation is 92% and rising to 94% in 2027, but utilisation is 58% in North-West Europe, 63% in North America and 60-70% in the rest of the world. Global utilisation falls from 72.2% to 71.3% in 2026 as a record 58m TEU of terminal capacity opens, the largest annual addition since 2008, and a further 36m TEU opens in 2027. APM Terminals' own utilisation fell to 81% from 86% as it added capacity.

Congestion that depends on typhoons and on Chinese yard delays is episodic, and the Q3 results showed that it is also expensive for Maersk.

Inference and so-what: the capacity tailwind halves within six to nine months, and the supply headwind peaks in 2028. The tailwind fades as Gemini completes its return to the Suez route (six services were back by September and a seventh in late October) and the remaining holdouts (Evergreen, HMM, Yang Ming and ONE) follow CMA CGM back. The supply headwind arrives in H1 2027 and peaks in 2028. On a six-month view the balance has already turned negative; on an eighteen-month view it is clearly negative.

Maersk's realised rate will fall faster than its peers' rates, because 56% of Maersk's volume is spot or short-contract, whereas Hapag-Lloyd carries 50-65% of its volume on contract.

Strongest counter-case

The bears have been early three years running: on the Red Sea in 2024, on tariff front-loading in 2025, and on Hormuz and congestion in 2026. A renewed disruption has arrived within twelve months of every forecast of normalisation since 2021. Deutsche Bank's congestion index showed no easing in late October, and carriers opened the 2027 contract season seeking increases. The new guidance implies Q4 2026 EBITDA of about 4.6-5.0bn, above Q3, which shows that management expects freight rates to hold through the winter.

What would change my view

Suez transits stalling below 60% of pre-crisis levels for two quarters.

Idle capacity rising above 3-4% and scrapping above 1% of the fleet within 2027; this would shorten the trough, not avert it.

A renewed Red Sea closure.

Market view against mine. The sell-side has fully articulated the direction of freight rates, but the share price has not priced it. I agree with the sell-side on direction, expect the turn sooner than the share price implies, and still give the disruption-extended case a full 20% probability.

Conclusion: the operating environment is a strong but fading and costly tailwind giving way to a strong, visible and structural headwind, and the balance is already negative on any horizon beyond the current quarter.
12

Score: 12, set by the Rater. The 2026 tailwind is temporary capacity absorption (Cape routing takes about 7% of the fleet, congestion 8.5-12.6%) that halves within six to nine months as the Suez route reopens, while a contracted supply wave (fleet growth of 7-9% in 2027 and 13% in 2028 against demand growth of 2-4%; an orderbook of 42-44%; scrapping near nil) removes about 5bn of EBITDA in FY2027 and 2.4bn more in FY2028. The consensus percentile figures (next-year EPS growth at the 0th percentile, sales growth at the 3.5th) tell the truth, and the 20% disruption-extended case delays the headwind rather than cancelling it. A strong, visible, structural net negative for two to three years: worse than Yara's reversing scarcity price, close to Fugro's, and in line with the External change forces group (13).

#2 Internally driven corporate change forces

Maersk's internal change is real, well resourced and mostly sensible, but the remaining self-help of about 0.8bn is an order of magnitude too small to offset the cycle, and the new fleet order is a step backwards in capital discipline.

Inference and so-what: self-help makes the trough shallower but does not change its sign or timing. The remaining self-help pool is about 0.8bn of EBITDA by FY2028 (Ocean network actions 0.55bn, overhead 0.18bn and filling Solutions' warehouse whitespace 0.1bn), or 1.1-1.3bn if losses deepen and management cuts harder. Against that pool, the erosion of the base freight rate removes about 5bn of EBITDA in FY2027 and a further 2.4bn in FY2028. Corporate change therefore makes the trough a few hundred million shallower and improves Maersk's position relative to its peers, but it does not change the sign or the timing of the trough.

Because of the fleet order and the fixed commitments, Maersk's capex and lease costs do not fall with its earnings: capex stays at 4.8-5.6bn a year through 2030.

Strongest counter-case

Maersk's downturn playbook is proven and larger than I model. In 2016 Maersk idled ships, returned chartered vessels, cut 4,000 roles and brought unit cost below USD 2,000 per FFE; in 2023 it cut 10,000 roles and reduced network cost by 14%. The new CFO's asset-light instincts could produce a capital markets day that reframes capex and targets, and the Terminals franchise compounds regardless of the cycle.

What would change my view

A deferral or resale of the newbuild slots.

A Logistics & Services margin above 6% for two quarters.

A cost programme of 1.5bn or more announced with the February 2027 guidance.

Market view against mine. The sell-side knows about the fleet order and the Solutions problem and gives Gemini its due. I agree, and add that Maersk's fixed commitments are larger than any broker models.

Conclusion: internal change is real, well resourced and mostly sensible, but it is an order of magnitude too small to matter against the cycle, and its newest element (fleet growth into a supply wave) is a regression in capital discipline.
44

Score: 44, set by the Rater. Gemini (950m of benefits delivered), the 3bn Terminals expansion, the Logistics reorganisation under new leaders from Kuehne+Nagel and the 1,000 roles cut are real, but the remaining self-help pool is only about 0.8bn by FY2028. Meanwhile Maersk's own 500k TEU order breaches its fleet cap at peak shipyard prices, market share has fallen to a twenty-year low, Solutions earns 1.7%, and the vessel-life change flatters reported EBIT. A mild net negative, a little below the Internal change forces group (46) because the fleet order and the fixed commitments lift the cost base within the three years; between Indus Holding's middling internal contribution and Xvivo's change undercut by internal problems.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Maersk is built to survive the cycle better than most carriers, not to escape it: its one moat, APM Terminals, carries much of the share price, and the market is still paying 15-20bn for an Ocean arm that will lose money at the EBIT level.

Industry structure: concentrated, but fragmented in behaviour whenever capacity is loose. The top five carriers hold 65% of capacity. In a loose market, however, prices are set by MSC (21.5% market share, with 2.9m TEU on order), CMA CGM and COSCO, none of which is run for listed-equity returns. Exit from the industry is blocked by 25-year vessel lives, state and family ownership, and the industry's cash.

Value chain: the value accrues to everyone except ocean carriers. Shipyards have full order books to 2029, terminals earn EBIT margins of about 33%, and asset-light forwarders earn high returns (DSV's ROIC is 15.4%). Ocean carriage does not: Maersk's ROIC was 5.7% in 2025 against a 7.5% target, and Hapag-Lloyd's was 4.6%.

Business model: one moat, one shared cost edge and one weak integrator strategy. APM Terminals is Maersk's one moat. Its revenue per container move grows about 7% a year on indexed concessions averaging 22 years, its ROIC is about 16% against a 9% hurdle, 63% of its revenue comes from third-party carriers, and its ROIC held at 10.5% in 2023 and 6.3% at the 2016 trough. That downturn record makes Terminals the group's earnings floor. Gemini gives Maersk a real but shared cost edge, 3-7% below non-Gemini carriers, which customers will capture as rates fall. The integrator model is a weak or even negative advantage: Maersk has spent more than 8bn on logistics acquisitions that earn below the cost of capital and still run on separate IT systems, and the model creates channel conflict with the forwarders who supply up to half of Ocean volume.

Financial profile: a strong balance sheet around weak earnings power. Net cash excluding leases is about 15.5bn, and the credit ratings are BBB+ (S&P) and Baa1 (Moody's). Yet company-basis free cash flow is barely positive even in a peak year, because capex (about 5bn) and lease repayments (3.5-3.9bn) absorb about 9bn a year. On my numbers, return on equity is 9% in FY2026, then 2%, -1%, 0% and 1% in FY2027-FY2030.

Management: a strong operator and a weak allocator of capital. Management executed Gemini well, has handled disruptions well and sets conservative formal guidance. Its capital allocation is weaker: pro-cyclical acquisitions, the fleet order, an accounting change that lifts reported EBIT, and no insider buying. The controlling family, with about 52% of the votes, offers stability and distributions, not capital discipline.

Inference and so-what: the sum of the parts shows what the market pays for Ocean. Terminals EBITDA of about 2.1bn at 10x, plus Logistics EBITDA of about 1.9bn at 7x, plus net cash, less leases and minorities, gives about USD 2,100-2,350 a share (DKK 14,000-15,700). At DKK 22,870, the market therefore pays roughly 15-20bn for an Ocean business that, on my numbers, loses money at the EBIT level from Q2 2027 to 2030.

Morgan Stanley's peer-multiple arithmetic puts the conglomerate discount on Terminals alone at about 14bn. That discount is the long-dated option in the stock, and the controlling family has shown with its oil, drilling and towage businesses that it will act on such discounts on its own timetable.

Strongest counter-case

The balance sheet lets Maersk invest and pay shareholders through a trough that will hurt weaker carriers such as ZIM. Gemini's hub concentration and the Terminals expansion deepen a structural cost and asset advantage. A margin-first turn by MSC, which happened in 2016-2017 once losses were widespread, would change the industry's conduct faster than I assume.

What would change my view

A separation or partial listing of Terminals.

Evidence that forwarders are returning cargo to Maersk in a loose market.

MSC or CMA CGM publicly idling capacity before losses force them to.

Market view against mine. The market and I agree that the industry structure is poor and that Terminals is the jewel. I differ in insisting that Maersk be valued on book value and the sum of the parts, not on a P/E that is meaningless for three years.

Conclusion: Maersk is a survivor-quality business in a structurally poor industry. Its one genuine moat, Terminals, is worth about 40% of the market value at 10x EBITDA and roughly two-thirds at the peer multiples behind Morgan Stanley's 14bn discount, while its Ocean arm is a price-taker for which the market still pays 15-20bn.
30

Score: 30, set by the Rater. A structurally poor, volume-first industry in which Ocean is a price-taker earning below its cost of capital through the cycle (ROIC 5.7% in 2025 against a 7.5% target; percentile figures: ROIC 28th, operating margin 16th, three-year margin change 1.8th), lifted by one genuine moat in APM Terminals (ROIC about 16%), a shared Gemini cost edge, net cash and a strong operating team that allocates capital poorly; predictability is among the lowest in the Universe. Coherent with the four groups (24, 34, 24, 38): a mediocre business made safe by its balance sheet, just above Instalco and below Zegona.

#4 Guidance conservatism, sell-side expectations and the delivery record

Management's guidance is conservative for the one quarter left in FY2026 and silent on FY2027, the year that matters; the FY2027 guidance due in early February 2027 is more likely to disappoint than to surprise.

Every FY2026 guidance raise marked the range to spot freight rates. The midpoint of FY2026 EBITDA guidance went from 5.75bn (February) to 9bn (29 June, an ad hoc update), 11.5bn (13 August) and 14.25bn (5 November). With Q3 EBITDA at 4.71bn and nine-month EBITDA at about 9.45bn, the new range implies Q4 EBITDA of about 4.6-5.0bn. None of the raises came from self-help.

Maersk sandbags in rising markets and guides accurately in falling ones. In rising markets Maersk sets its initial ranges wide and low (1-6bn of EBITDA in February 2024; an EBIT loss in February 2026) and lets the market discover the rest. In falling markets its initial guidance came in below consensus and proved right or conservative (February 2016, 2019 and 2024); Maersk halved its dividend in 2017 and suspended its buyback in 2024.

The sell-side sits at the top of the largest upgrade cycle in Europe, and it is deeply divided. FY2027 consensus EPS rose 459% in three months, and the FY2026 mean went from USD -55 to +487 in a year. Yet only 8% of ratings are Buy, and three of the five most active houses rated the shares Sell or Underperform until DNB Carnegie upgraded to Hold after Q3. Dispersion is extreme: FY2027 EPS estimates run from USD -22 to +497, and FY2028 EBITDA estimates from 1.5bn to 10.2bn.

Inference for FY2026: the guidance is a floor, and the remaining quarter carries little risk. I set FY2026 EBITDA at 14.05bn, the bottom of the range, because I expect Asia-Europe rates to roll over within Q4, while management's record says the bottom of a November range holds.

Inference for FY2027: the February 2027 guidance is the single most important date in the next eighteen months, and it is more likely to be negative than positive for the shares. Maersk gives no FY2027 guidance until early February 2027, and its record says that guidance will be set wide and low. I expect a FY2027 EBITDA range of roughly 6-9bn, with a midpoint below the 9.3bn consensus and near my 8.4bn, an EBIT range near zero, guidance for negative company-basis free cash flow and, more likely than not, no new buyback.

Maersk's delivery record offers no comfort. Its 2026 beats coincided with beats at Hapag-Lloyd, COSCO, HMM, ZIM and NYK, so they reflect the freight market rather than Maersk's execution, and Maersk's one differentiator, its higher exposure to spot rates, works against it in 2027.

Strongest counter-case

DNB Carnegie now expects the 2027 guidance to be "stronger than initial expectations" because near-term demand is resilient. The Q4 exit rate implied by guidance (USD 3,200 or more per FFE) carries into Q1 2027, and the contract book could lock in more of it. Management has never cut an in-year range under the current CEO, Vincent Clerc.

What would change my view

A February 2027 range with a midpoint at or above 9bn.

An ad hoc guidance raise before February.

Asia-Europe contracts settling within 10% of 2026 levels.

Market view against mine. The market reads each guidance raise as evidence that earnings are durable. I read each raise as a lagging thermometer of spot rates, and note that the November raise was the first that the shares did not reward.

Conclusion: guidance is conservative for the quarter that remains and silent on the year that matters, the upgrade record belongs to the freight rate rather than to management, and the next guidance event is more likely to disappoint than to surprise.
47

Score: 47, set by the Rater. The guidance mechanics are honest and conservative (initial ranges wide and low, never an in-year cut under Clerc, falling-market guidance that proved right), but every 2026 raise marked guidance to spot rates, Q3 missed consensus EBITDA by about 14%, and the FY2027 guidance in February is likely to land below a consensus that sits at the top of a +477% revision cycle (Sell-side estimates group 16). An honest tracker whose record belongs to the freight rate, held below the middle of the scale by the Q3 miss and the coming below-consensus guidance; between Sdiptech and Instalco.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Maersk's Ocean business combines extreme operating leverage with no pricing power of its own, so a 17% revenue decline in FY2027 becomes a 75% fall in EBIT; the only leverage working in Maersk's favour is the small, positive leverage in Terminals.

Pricing power: none in Ocean, real in Terminals. Maersk's realised Ocean rates track the spot indices with a beta of about 0.4-0.5 and a one-quarter lag: they fell 14% year on year in Q1 2026 while the Drewry index fell 32%, and rose 32% quarter on quarter in Q2 while the SCFI rose 55%. Only niche shippers pay a premium for reliability; in one industry expert's words, "95% of standard customers buy the cheapest rate". Reliability also improves exactly when capacity is loose, which is when nobody pays for it. Terminals, by contrast, has real pricing power: revenue per move rises about 7% a year on indexed concessions, matching labour-cost inflation of 7%.

Operating leverage: price leverage on a cost base that is fixed per sailing. Terminal handling is 39% of Ocean costs and varies with each container; network costs excluding bunker are 27% and fixed per sailing; bunker fuel is 19% and is passed through to customers via the Fossil Fuel Fee, which recovers 80-90% of the cost in a tight market and about 70% in a loose one; SG&A is 9%. On top of these costs sits 6.25-7.0bn of annual depreciation. As a result, a 1% move in the Ocean rate is worth about 0.35bn of EBIT.

Revenue is a poor guide to profit. In FY2027 Maersk's revenue falls about 17%, but about USD 290 per FFE of that decline is pass-through surcharges and fuel recovery, which leave together with the costs they cover. The decline that hits profit is the erosion of the base rate, about USD 380 per FFE.

Financial leverage: nil today, and turning into a drag. Each 1bn of cash consumed costs about 40m of pre-tax income, lease interest of about 0.7bn a year does not fall with earnings, and the buyback, which added about 2% a year to EPS, stops.

The Q3 lesson: leverage is symmetric, and congestion is a mixed blessing. In Q3 2026 the rate rose 46% year on year, but unit cost at constant fuel prices rose 5% because of congestion and lower volume, so EBITDA missed consensus by 14% even at a record rate. When congestion clears, costs fall with it, but so does the rate, and the rate is worth four to five times as much to profit as the cost line.

Feedback loops: three reinforce the downturn, two reverse themselves.

  • Reinforcing the downturn. High profits feed the orderbook, which is already locked in for 2027-2028. The industry's cash buffer delays scrapping until losses are widespread: in 2015-2016 scrapping rose from 197k to 657k TEU only after a year of losses. Shorter contracts transmit spot rates into realised rates within a quarter, in both directions.
  • Self-reversing. Route disruption reverses because each carrier that returns to the Suez route gains a cost edge and pressures the rest to follow. Congestion reverses because softer volumes clear port queues.
  • Compounding for Maersk. Gemini directs volume into Maersk-owned hub terminals.
  • Costing Maersk. The conflict between Maersk's integrator model and the forwarders costs about one point of volume a year in a loose market.

Inference and so-what: operating leverage is about to run backwards. The rule that revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth holds for Maersk, and in FY2027 it reverses: on my numbers revenue falls 17%, EBITDA 40%, EBIT 75% and EPS 77%. The genuinely margin-accretive cost-out (about 0.8bn) is a tenth of the pass-through cost pool (4-5bn) and a sixth of the base-rate erosion.

Strongest counter-case

Positive leverage exists in Terminals, where price per move rises faster than cost, and in Solutions, where filling warehouse whitespace is worth 0.1-0.15bn by 2028. Gemini's cost edge keeps Maersk's Ocean EBITDA positive (about USD 165 per FFE) at a rate that puts the marginal carrier into a cash loss. Carriers abandon slow steaming when Brent falls below USD 100, which re-releases capacity in a falling oil market; equally, a high oil price would re-absorb that capacity.

What would change my view

Realised rates falling by less than half the index decline through two quarters of 2027, which would show a contract or reliability cushion.

The Fossil Fuel Fee holding 90% recovery in a loose market.

Market view against mine. The market prices Maersk's leverage to EBITDA correctly and ignores its leverage below EBIT.

Conclusion: extreme, symmetric price leverage with no pricing power behind it means the business model turns revenue declines into disproportionate profit declines from Q1 2027, and the only leverage working in Maersk's favour is the small, positive leverage in Terminals.
32

Score: 32, set by the Rater. The structure has extreme operating gearing (a cost base fixed per sailing, so 1% on the Ocean rate is about 0.35bn of EBIT) but no pricing power of its own in Ocean (realised rates track the indices at a beta of 0.4-0.5); real pricing power exists only in Terminals; financial leverage is nil and turning into a drag (interest income decaying, the buyback ending); cost-out of about 0.8bn faces 4-5bn of erosion; and the feedback loops reinforce the downturn. Gearing without pricing power that is about to run backwards (FY2027 revenue -17%, EBIT -75%) sits between the 25 and 50 levels; net cash and the cost-out scope keep it off the 10 level.

Upside counter-case: disruption-extended (about 20%)

A renewed closure holds FY2027 rates near USD 2,600 per FFE, EBITDA at about 14bn and EPS at USD 500 or more, and consensus rises again. The orderbook then pushes the trough into 2028-2029 rather than cancelling it.

Downside case: deeper downturn (about 30%)

Rates fall to about USD 1,800 in 2027 and 1,650 in 2028; EBITDA is 3.7bn and 3.1bn; FY2028 EPS is about USD -250 to -300; net cash excluding leases is near zero by 2029; and an Ocean impairment becomes certain, because impairment headroom was only 1.1bn at end-2025 (down from 4.1bn) after the vessel-life extension lifted carrying values.

What would change my view: idle capacity above 4% and scrapping above 1% of the fleet by mid-2027, which would confine the trough to 2028 and make 2029 a recovery year.

Market view against mine. Consensus has the shape of the cycle right but the level too high from FY2027, most of all at EPS. Its FY2029 figure is two brokers' extrapolation, not a considered view.

Conclusion: the outlook is a lower, flatter plateau rather than a V, with EBITDA 10-17% below consensus and EPS near zero or negative for three years, and with no scope for growth or for margins above the past until a 2030 recovery that only returns EBITDA to about the FY2027 level.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and narrative over 6-12 months

The scope for upgrades is one quarter wide and largely priced, while the scope for downgrades covers three forecast years and is concentrated in the February 2027 guidance; over 6-12 months the balance points clearly toward estimate cuts.

The calendar of the next fifteen months is weighted to the downside. Maersk B enters the OMX Nordic 40 index on 1 December, which brings passive buying, partly offset by SEK 240m of index selling in the Copenhagen index rebalancing. Asia-Europe contracts settle from December to February. In early February 2027 Maersk reports FY2026 results and gives its first FY2027 guidance, together with the FY2026 dividend (about USD 194, or DKK 1,300, a 5.7% yield) and the buyback decision, which management has explicitly deferred until then. The Transpacific contract season follows in May. The Q1 2027 results in May will still show year-on-year growth of about 13% on my path; the Q2 2027 results in August will show the first year-on-year decline, about -14%, as the 2027 ship deliveries arrive.

Where consensus stands after Q3. FY2026 consensus sits roughly at the guidance midpoint. FY2027 consensus EBITDA is about 9.3bn: DNB Carnegie raised its estimate 17% to 9.1bn, while Morgan Stanley's forecast of a 45% decline from 14.25bn implies about 7.8bn. FY2027 EPS estimates include Deutsche Bank's USD 83, Morgan Stanley's 74 and Bernstein's 86. FY2028 consensus EBITDA is still the pre-Q3 figure of 7.5bn.

Upgrade scope is confined to Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. In those two quarters, the exit rate and any contract book signed at today's levels could beat a cautious February range.

Downgrade scope covers FY2027, FY2028 and FY2029. For FY2027, my 8.4bn compares with 9.3bn, and the EPS cut will be larger as brokers model the tax floor and the end of the buyback. For FY2028, my 6.3bn compares with 7.5bn, with economic EBIT at zero. For FY2029, a consensus median will form at 6.5-7.5bn as 18 brokers roll their models forward, which will register as a cut even though no broker cuts. I put the probability that net FY2027 revisions are negative at about 70% over the three months to end-February (lower than before Q3, because the exit rate is higher) and at about 85% over twelve months.

Capital allocation is the one two-sided event. With net cash excluding leases above 16bn at year-end, a token 0.5-1bn buyback is about 45% likely, and a 2bn programme (Morgan Stanley's expectation) perhaps 15% likely. The market would read either as a positive against my base case of no buyback.

The narrative will turn against a long position. Nearly all the items that will enter the story over the next 6-12 months are negative: trough EPS turning out negative rather than the consensus +62, the Ocean impairment flag in the February annual report, the quarterly shape of 2027, and the fixed lease and fuel commitments. The positives not yet written (a 2029-2030 recovery on scrapping and falling deliveries, and the Terminals discount) are 18-30 months from appearing in reported numbers.

Strongest counter-case

The disruption-extended case would keep revisions positive into mid-2027, bring the bulls (Clarksons, Goldman Sachs and UBS) to the fore, and force the bears to capitulate on timing, as in 2024 and 2025. A strong contract season would do half of this on its own.

What would change my view

Asia-Europe contracts at or above 2026 levels.

An ad hoc guidance raise before February.

Suez transits stalling.

Market view against mine. The market expects continued strength through Q4 and a reset at some point in 2027. I expect the reset to be guided in February and to become visible in the Q2 2027 results, with the February guidance as the pivot.

Conclusion: the scope for upgrades is one quarter wide and already largely in the price, while the scope for downgrades covers three forecast years and is concentrated in the February 2027 guidance; the balance over 6-12 months is clearly toward cuts.

#8 Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative and price, and at peers

Every momentum measure is at or near its maximum, and the first crack has appeared where it matters most: a record quarter and a guidance raise did not lift the shares.

Guidance momentum has cracked. Maersk raised guidance three times in five months, and the last raise was the first that the shares did not reward. Morgan Stanley wrote "guidance upgrade not enough to support shares", and DNB Carnegie upgraded to Hold citing "lack of catalyst; valuation reset".

Estimate momentum is at its peak. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum A. FY2027 consensus EPS rose 128% in one month and 459% in three. Target prices rose 41% in three months but remain 13% below the share price, and the Buy share is unchanged at 8%.

Price momentum is at its peak. The dashboard rates technical momentum A, and relative strength is in the 97th percentile. The 200-day moving average has risen for twelve months, while the 50-day average (DKK 22,926) sits almost exactly at the price. Morgan Stanley's strategy team ranks Maersk second in Europe on twelve-month idiosyncratic momentum (155%).

Positioning has already been cleaned out. Short interest reached 33% of the free float in August 2025 and was then squeezed; Deutsche Bank describes quant deleveraging and algorithmic short covering. On 6 November Deutsche Bank reported systematic positioning at neutral and discretionary positioning at the bottom of its range.

Peers: the rally is sector-wide, but Maersk's closest freight peer has not joined it. The shipping cohort rose 82% over twelve months. Wallenius Wilhelmsen (+118%) and Hoegh Autoliners (+106%) show the same dashboard grade profile (A/A/F or B/C/F) at the 100th P/E percentile. Hapag-Lloyd, Maersk's Gemini partner in the same freight market, rose only 10.7% and carries a D for technical momentum. Among the forwarders, DSV grades F/F/A at the 2nd percentile and Kuehne+Nagel A/A/D. The wider market is risk-off, defensives lead cyclicals, and the house momentum tilt has moved to underweight.

Inference and so-what: in past cycles the share price peaked with the freight rate, and the rate has already peaked. In previous cycles Maersk's share price peaked within zero to two months of the freight-index peak, and consensus peaked with the rate. The SCFI peaked at 3,590 in early September 2026, and the B share peaked near DKK 24,900 shortly afterwards. Sell-side earnings momentum will fall from A within one or two quarters as the FY2027 cuts begin, and price momentum typically turns first. Because the position is crowded and idiosyncratic, the next 10-20% move in the shares can happen without any company news.

Strongest counter-case

Momentum can persist for quarters. The OMX Nordic 40 inclusion brings passive buying. Residual short positions, invisible below the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority's 0.5% disclosure threshold, can be squeezed again on any disruption headline. The 50-day moving average has held through every pullback in 2026.

What would change my view

A close above the 52-week high of DKK 25,380 on a disruption event would extend the momentum phase.

A break below the 50-day average followed by the 150-day average (DKK 18,442) would confirm the turn.

Market view against mine. The dashboard and the market rate momentum A across the board. I agree with the reading and disagree about its durability.

Conclusion: momentum is at its maximum on every measure and has just failed its first test, which in Maersk's own history marks a top rather than the start of a new leg up.
90

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth, with guidance raised three times, FY2027 EPS up 459% in three months and the price 30% above a rising 200-day average, give an A. I place it at the floor of the A band because the narrative has cracked (the latest raise was the first the shares did not reward), Buy ratings stay at 8% with targets 13% below the price, and the closest freight peer, Hapag-Lloyd, lags.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The investment case is simple and cheap to track, but its earnings level is unusually fragile and the share price can move suddenly; historical precedent supports a downside skew on price.

The case is simple. It has one driver: the Ocean base rate, net of pass-through items. It has two causes: the orderbook, which is certain and plays out over years, and the timing of the Suez return, which is uncertain and plays out over quarters. It has one transmission constant (USD 100 per FFE = about 1.36bn of EBITDA = about USD 95 of EPS) and three small below-EBIT items that decide the sign of EPS.

The case is cheap to monitor in near real time. The most important single reading is Maersk's own Q4 2026 loaded rate against about USD 3,200 per FFE: a rate above 3,000 would say the disruption-extended case is live, and a rate below 2,700 would say the base case has arrived early.

The level of earnings is fragile. The FY2027 EBITDA range runs from 3.7bn to 14.5bn around my 8.4bn, and the sell-side's own FY2027 EPS estimates run from USD -22 to +497. A band of only USD 150-200 per FFE in the rate decides whether FY2028 EPS is positive or negative, and even at the February 2028 results the top of the range of FY2028 outcomes will still be about twice the bottom.

The downside path needs no company capability at all; 2016 and 2023 are the templates. The floor under the forecast rests on capabilities already in the accounts: Gemini's cost position, Terminals and net cash. The one assumption that could make the forecast wrong on the upside is management's landside thesis.

Headline risk is high and two-sided. A ceasefire, a Suez Canal Authority statement, a Hormuz incident, a weekly index print, a peer's profit warning or an ad hoc Danish stock-exchange disclosure can each move the shares 10-20% within days. Dated risk clusters in February 2027: the guidance, the buyback decision and the impairment headroom.

Lower-probability company-specific risks are an Ocean impairment at the FY2027 test (non-cash, and more likely than not on my numbers); 4.6bn of logistics goodwill, newly reallocated across three units, which exposes Solutions; a failure at a Gemini hub; a cyber attack (the 2017 NotPetya attack cost 250-300m); antitrust action against shipping alliances; a forwarder boycott; and a German tax audit of how shipping income is allocated.

Cyclical precedent: the share price leads the earnings trough by six to twenty-four months and follows the rate peak within two months. In 2015-2016 the share price peaked almost two years before the earnings trough and the stock reached 0.4-0.5x book. In 2022-2023 the price troughed one month after the freight-index bottom. In 2024-2026 every forecast of normalisation was overtaken by a new disruption.

What would change my view on riskiness

A multi-year contract book covering more than 60% of volume, as at Hapag-Lloyd, which would slow the transmission of spot rates and narrow the range of outcomes.

Market view against mine

The sell-side grades the risk as I do; the share price grades it as low.

Conclusion: the case is simple and trackable but unusually fragile in level and sudden in price, with a range of outcomes among the widest relative to market value of any European large cap, and with a downside skew on price that historical precedent supports.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock sits at the top of its Reinforcing phase; the transition to Stalling is already visible in the reaction to Q3, and the next phase for the price is Collapsing, not Broadening.

The dashboard's rule says Reinforcing. Momentum is A, sell-side momentum is A, guidance has been raised three times, and the two-year-forward multiple is at its 90-month maximum.

The fundamentals say the Reinforcing phase is ending. The latest results missed on EBITDA, EBIT and volume; the shares did not respond to a guidance raise; the implied Q4 2026 is the last quarter of rising year-on-year rates on any plausible path; and the February 2027 guidance will be set below consensus. Above all, the input force (capacity absorption) is reversing while the output (reported earnings) is still rising, the classic gap between a turning input and a lagging output.

Inference: the price is likely to trough in 2027, a year before earnings. I expect the stock to tip from Reinforcing into Stalling between now and February 2027, and then into Collapsing in price terms through H1 2027 as the FY2027 guidance and the Q2 2027 year-on-year decline arrive. Bottoming becomes plausible from mid-2028, when scrapping engages, the 2028 delivery peak passes, and the market can see deliveries falling after 2029 alongside Maersk's own 2029-2030 newbuilds. Because the price troughs six to twelve months before earnings, the price trough is more likely in 2027 than in 2028. The "turning up" narrative (scrapping, a cleaner balance sheet, a re-rated Terminals business) does not yet exist in print; it will be written from mid-2028.

Strongest counter-case and what would change my view

A renewed disruption would extend Reinforcing by two to four quarters, as in 2024 and 2025. The signal would be a new high above DKK 25,380 with FY2027 consensus EBITDA moving above 11bn.

Market view against mine

The dashboard's mechanical rule and the share price say Reinforcing; the sell-side's ratings say Stalling or Collapsing. I side with the sell-side on fundamentals and sit one to two quarters ahead of the price.

Conclusion: the stock is at the top of its Reinforcing phase, the transition to Stalling is already visible in the reaction to Q3, and the next phase for the price is Collapsing rather than Broadening.

The computed Reinforcing phase is right only at its top: the input force (capacity absorption) is reversing while reported earnings still rise, Q3 missed and a raise was not rewarded, and the next six to twelve months bring the first year-on-year decline (Q2 2027) and a below-consensus guide, tipping the stock into Stalling and then Collapsing in price terms. A windfall at its peak with the first decline ahead: below Imperial Brands' Stalling-to-Collapsing and above Judges Scientific's confirmed Collapsing, because Maersk's earnings have not yet turned down.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline 22x P/E works only on through-cycle earnings, where it gives the same DKK 14,000-17,000 as 0.5-0.6x book and the sum of the parts; the fair multiple is therefore about 0.55x book, about 30% below the current price.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a stock in the Reinforcing phase is the 90th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E. For Maersk that is 22.0x (10th percentile 10.2x, median 15.0x, 75th percentile 18.3x), against 92.5x today. The Financial Analyst's model applies 22x to two-year-forward EPS at each horizon.

The P/E is the wrong instrument for Maersk now, for a reason the model itself exposes. Two-year-forward EPS is near zero or negative in FY2028-FY2029, so 22x produces a negative value per share and a "return" of about -102% that carries no information (topic #12). Three alternative methods agree with each other:

  1. Through-cycle earnings. 22x applied to a mid-cycle EPS of about USD 100-110 gives USD 2,200-2,400, or DKK 14,700-16,000. That mid-cycle EPS is roughly the 2020 or 2023-2025 level excluding disruption years, and close to the average of my FY2027-FY2030 path once FY2030 is treated as the normal year.
  2. Book value. The industry's trough band is 0.4-0.5x book (Morgan Stanley's floor is 0.4x; Maersk fell to 0.5x in past panics and stood at 0.6x in August 2026), and its peak is 1.0x or above. A stock entering its trough with the earnings turn still ahead deserves the lower half of that range, and 0.5-0.6x on FY2027 book value of about USD 4,250 a share gives DKK 14,000-17,000.
  3. The sum of the parts. Valuing Ocean at nil gives DKK 14,000-15,700. Bernstein's mid-cycle 0.7x enterprise value to invested capital gives DKK 16,250; DNB Carnegie's 0.8x sum of the parts (Ocean at 0.5x, Logistics at 8x EBITDA) gives DKK 19,600; and Deutsche Bank's target price is DKK 19,010.

My fair value is therefore DKK 14,000-17,000, central DKK 15,500, about 0.55x book. I adjust for the phase: if Maersk were genuinely in a peak-delivery phase with upgrades ahead, 0.8-1.0x book (DKK 22,000-28,000) would be defensible. In a Stalling-to-Collapsing phase, with a range of outcomes this wide, the lower half of the historical range is the right place.

Strongest counter-case and what would change my view

The disruption-extended case justifies 1.0x book (DKK 28,000) for as long as it lasts. A Terminals separation would re-rate the parts. A demonstrated structural floor under freight rates (two consecutive supply-wave quarters with the SCFI above 2,000) would move my central value toward 0.7x book.

Market view against mine

The market pays about 0.8x book, and the most active sell-side houses cluster at 0.7-0.8x (DKK 16,250-19,600). I sit at the low end of the sell-side because I treat the squeeze below EBIT and the fixed commitments as real.

Conclusion: the guideline 22x is only meaningful on through-cycle earnings, where it lands at the same DKK 14,000-17,000 as 0.5-0.6x book and a sum of the parts with Ocean at nil, so the fair multiple is about 0.55x book, about 30% below the current price.

Both readings are inflated by near-zero two-year-forward EPS, so I lift the score a little within the band; but on the memo's better instrument, book value, the stock still trades at about 0.8x against a fair 0.55x for a stock entering its trough, so the dearness is real, and the Stalling-to-Collapsing phase deserves it.

#12 Total shareholder return, by the DuPont split

The base-case total return is about -25% over eighteen months and about -13% over three years, almost entirely from de-rating; only the 20% disruption-extended case gives a positive return.

The model's figure, and why I set it aside. At the guideline 22x, the Financial Analyst's model gives a total return of about -102% to the eighteen-month horizon (31 December 2027) and about -58% to the three-year horizon (30 June 2029), with a negative value per share at the first horizon. That result is 22x applied to negative two-year-forward EPS. It proves that the P/E cannot value this stock through the trough; it is not a return forecast.

Base case, eighteen months to mid-2028: about -25%.

  • Value: 0.55x book on FY2027 book value of about USD 4,250 a share gives USD 2,340, or DKK 15,600.
  • Book value per share: about -1%. FY2027 earnings of about 1.6bn roughly offset the 2.8bn FY2026 dividend and the FY2028 loss.
  • Multiple: -31%, from 0.8x to 0.55x book; with book value flat, the share price falls about 32%.
  • Dividends: about +7% (DKK 1,300 for FY2026, paid in March 2027, and about DKK 300 for FY2027, paid in March 2028).

Through the P/E lens the same move appears as two-year-forward EPS falling from about USD 33 (the FY2027-FY2028 blend) to about USD 19 (the FY2029-FY2030 blend) while the multiple collapses from 92x to a figure that is still meaningless. The book-value lens is the one to use.

Three years, to late 2029: about -13%, or about -4.5% a year. By late 2029 the market looks at FY2030 (EBITDA 8.5bn, EPS about USD 52), scrapping is under way, deliveries are falling, and the balance sheet still holds about 6-7bn of net cash excluding leases. A turning-up multiple of 0.6-0.7x on book value of about USD 4,200 a share gives DKK 16,800-19,600, central DKK 18,200 (-20%); adding the same 7% of dividends (nothing is paid for FY2028-FY2029) gives about -13%. The three-year return is better than the eighteen-month return because the price trough most likely falls in 2027 and a recovery multiple has begun to form by late 2029.

Scenario-weighted, eighteen months: about -20%. Base case (50%): about -25%. Deeper downturn (30%): 0.4x book, DKK 11,200, with the FY2026 dividend paid, about -45%. Disruption-extended (20%): 1.0x book, DKK 28,000, plus a larger dividend, about +28%. The downside case is both larger (-45% against +28%) and more probable (30% against 20%) than the upside case, and the share price already sits at the top of the range.

The multiple drives the return, overwhelmingly. The de-rating contributes -31 points, against -1 for book value and +7 for dividends. Earnings growth contributes nothing, because the stock moves from the top of its price-to-book range to the lower half while book value stays flat. The dividend is a real but one-off cushion, worth under a third of the expected de-rating.

Where the positive return liesThe return would be positive only if the disruption-extended case held the multiple at 0.8-1.0x book through 2027, or for an investor who buys the trough. A move from 0.45x book (about DKK 12,500) to 0.8x book (about DKK 22,500) over 2028-2030 would return 75-80% plus dividends. That trough purchase is the setup this memo recommends Richard prepares for.
Conclusion: the base-case total return is about -25% over eighteen months and about -13% over three years, almost entirely a de-rating from 0.8x to 0.55-0.65x book, partly cushioned by a 5.7% FY2026 dividend and not cushioned by earnings at all; the scenario-weighted eighteen-month return is about -20%.

I move the score down one point for the fat, correlated lower tail (the 30% deeper case at -45%, with an Ocean impairment cutting book value) and for a three-year check that is also negative, against a 20% upside case of about +28%.

The five judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic

Every judgement uses the same transmission constants. USD 100 per FFE on the annual Ocean rate equals about 1.36bn of EBITDA and EBIT (on 13.6m FFE), which equals about USD 95 of EPS after a near-zero marginal tax rate, on 14.34m shares. One quarter's rate applies to about 3.35m FFE.

1. The FY2027 average loaded rate (base about USD 2,150 per FFE) spans the whole sell-side range and the whole range of share-price outcomes. If the year averages 2,600 because the disruption persists: +450 x 13.6m = +6.1bn of EBITDA, to about 14.5bn; EBIT about 8.0bn; EPS +425, to about 540; free cash flow positive and a buyback probable. If it averages 1,800 because a 2016-type price war coincides with a fast Suez return: -350 x 13.6m = -4.8bn, to about 3.6bn of EBITDA; EBIT about -2.9bn; EPS -330, to about -220; company-basis free cash flow about -6bn.

2. The timing of the reset within H1 2027 (base: Q1 rate 2,600, Q2 rate 2,200) decides where the February guidance lands. If the Asia-Europe contract book settles near 2026 levels and Q1 2027 realises 3,000 and Q2 2,500: (+400 + 300) x 3.35m = +2.3bn of FY2027 EBITDA, to about 10.7bn, which is above today's consensus; EPS rises by about 160 to about 270, and the February guidance range would likely be set 1-2bn higher. The H2 2027 and 2028 path would be unchanged or worse, as the delayed capacity release meets the new deliveries. If instead Q1 realises 2,300 and Q2 2,000 because the Suez return is fast in Q4-Q1: -1.7bn of EBITDA, EPS down about 115 to about zero, and the February guidance would straddle an EBIT loss.

3. The FY2028 trough rate (base 1,905, about 1,400 fuel-adjusted) decides the sign of trough EPS within a narrow band. A 2019-type moderate trough at 2,100: +195 x 13.9m = +2.7bn, to about 9.0bn of EBITDA; EBIT about +2.5bn; EPS +185, to about +140; consensus would be roughly vindicated. A 2016-type trough at 1,650: -255 x 13.9m = -3.5bn, to about 2.8bn of EBITDA; EBIT about -3.7bn; EPS -245, to about -290; an Ocean impairment would be certain, and net cash excluding leases would fall to about 2-3bn by 2029. The band that decides the sign of trough EPS is narrower than the move in the realised rate in any of the last six quarters.

4. The below-EBIT items in a near-zero year (FY2028 base EPS -46) move the centre of the range by about USD 60 a share. The per-share bridge from EBIT to EPS is EBIT including joint ventures +12 (which contains the vessel-life benefit of +49), net interest and other -24, tax -28 and minorities -7. If the sell-side's implicit assumptions held instead (tax at about 10% of pre-tax profit, and so near nil on a loss; interest income flat at the FY2026 level; buybacks of 1bn a year continuing), FY2028 EPS would be about -46 + 28 + 14 + 3 = about zero, which is roughly where the economic consensus sits. Reversing the vessel-life change would take EPS to about -95. These items do not change the width of the range of outcomes; they move its centre by about USD 60 a share, which is the whole gap between a "moderate trough" and "losses".

5. Capital allocation in February 2027 (base: a dividend of about DKK 1,300 and no new buyback) is a signal, not an earnings driver. A 1bn buyback would reduce the share count by about 2% and add about USD 2-3 to FY2028 EPS, which is immaterial, but the market would read it as a signal that the balance sheet (net cash excluding leases above 16bn at year-end), rather than the cycle, sets distributions; Morgan Stanley's 2bn case would be a 4% signal of the same kind. A dividend cut of the 2017 kind (50%) for FY2027 is already implied by my USD 45 a share.

The Ocean impairment is the balance-sheet event in the other direction. Impairment headroom is 1.1bn, and a 0.5-point change in the discount rate is worth about 2.7bn. An impairment would be non-cash and outside underlying EPS, but it would produce a reported loss of several billion and a lower book value for the price-to-book anchor, partly offset by about 0.2bn a year of lower depreciation.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Maersk is a well-run, well-financed survivor of a structurally poor industry, at the top of a disruption-driven earnings cycle whose one driver is about to reverse. Maersk has used its best years to build the two assets that will carry it through the trough: Gemini's cost position and APM Terminals' compounding, scarce assets. It has also spent those years on a fleet order and fixed commitments that keep capex and lease costs high while earnings fall. The Q3 2026 results were the first evidence that earnings supported by congestion carry their own costs, and the guidance raise that came with them was the first the shares did not reward.

Over twelve to twenty-four months the investment case is negative in direction with high confidence, and unknowable in level. The FY2027 freight rate decides everything: the orderbook makes the direction certain, the timing of the Suez return makes the quarter uncertain, and three below-EBIT items that nobody has added together make trough EPS negative rather than mildly positive. The shares, at about 0.8x book and at the 100th percentile of their P/E range, discount the upside scenario. The sell-side has written the bear case in full but not its arithmetic below EBIT, and the February 2027 guidance is the pivot.

My fair value is DKK 14,000-17,000, and my base-case eighteen-month return is about -25% (about -20% scenario-weighted). The better Maersk setup is the one that forms in 2027-2028 at 0.4-0.5x book, when scrapping begins and the delivery wave peaks: a quality cyclical at a trough-on-trough setup, to be bought then and not anticipated now.

10Thesis's change forces' strength
30Foundations' robustness
8Setups' fit and crispness
18Case riskiness

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 10, set by the Rater. One overwhelming external blow (a contracted record supply wave meeting the unwinding of the Red Sea buffer; topic 1 at 12) is met by mildly negative internal change (topic 2 at 44) and reaches profits with high certainty, because EPS falls from about 486 to negative in FY2028-FY2029 (topic 6, an F at 5); the direction is near-certain even though the level is not.

Foundations' Robustness: 30, set by the Rater. A mediocre, price-taking Ocean business in a structurally poor industry is made safe by net cash and a genuine Terminals moat (topic 3 at 30), with an honest but rate-driven guidance record (topic 4 at 47) that neither lifts nor sinks it; its margins and returns are among the least stable in the Universe, the opposite of the stability that lifts a business with ordinary returns.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 8, set by the Rater. In substance the case is the inverse of a Target Setup: a windfall at its peak with the earnings turn one to two quarters ahead, exactly the point at which the quality-cyclical trough-on-trough setup would sell; the business's current problems (share loss, the fleet order, congestion costs) blur even that later fit, and the setup it could become is twelve to twenty-four months away.

Case Riskiness: 18, set by the Rater. Simple and trackable fundamentals with no balance-sheet risk do not offset a next-year EPS range that spans losses to profits, sudden 10-20% headline moves, a crowded position and a peak multiple (topic 9 at 17); net cash keeps it off the 10 level.

Price basis. Prepared 8 November 2026 for Richard. The share price basis is DKK 22,870, the dashboard's price on 23 October 2026 (USD 3,428 at DKK/USD 6.67), giving a market value of about USD 50bn on 14.6m shares; per-share earnings use 14.34m shares. The Q3 2026 results of 5 November and the guidance raise that came with them are in the source files; the share price data end on 23 October, so every return figure is measured from DKK 22,870.

Forecast sources. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2) with the changes set out in inputs-changed.md: Q3 2026 set to the actual (underlying EBITDA 4.71bn); Q4 2026 and H1 2027 lifted for the Q3 results and the new FY2026 guidance, with the FY2026 and FY2027 tax rates and dividends following; and FY2028 revenue growth adjusted so that the FY2028-FY2030 trough and recovery levels are unchanged. The resulting base case is the table in topic #6.

Figures that differ between sources. The model's eighteen-month total return at 22x is -102.4% on its one-page summary (chart in topic #12) and -104% in the analyst's draft; the three-year figure is -58.2% on the summary and -60% (-29% a year) in the draft. The scenario-weighted eighteen-month return is about -20% on rounded scenario returns and -21% on unrounded ones. The three-month rise in FY2027 consensus EPS is +459% in the analyst's evidence and +477% in the Rater's reason for topic #4. FY2027 EBITDA in the deeper case is 3.7bn in the scenario chart and about 3.6bn in the arithmetic of judgement 1. In topic #3, "roughly two-thirds of the share price" for Terminals holds at peer multiples (20.6bn plus Morgan Stanley's 14bn discount, against about 50bn); at 10x EBITDA Terminals is about 40% of the market value.

Glossary.

FFE / TEUForty-foot / twenty-foot equivalent unit, the standard measures of container volume and ship capacity. SCFI, Drewry WCI, CCFIShanghai Containerized Freight Index, Drewry World Container Index and China Containerized Freight Index: spot freight-rate indices. GeminiMaersk's network partnership with Hapag-Lloyd, launched in 2025. Fossil Fuel FeeMaersk's surcharge that passes bunker fuel costs through to customers. Tonnage taxA regime that taxes shipping on fleet size rather than on profit, so Ocean earnings carry almost no marginal tax. Vessel-life benefitThe roughly 0.7bn a year of lower depreciation from Maersk's extension of its vessels' useful lives. Company-basis free cash flowFree cash flow after capex and lease repayments. Lifecycle phasesViewforth's stages for a stock: Broadening, Reinforcing, Stalling, Collapsing and Bottoming.

Scores and visuals. The Rater set every topic score, the reason given with it and the four theme scores in topic #13. Default visuals come from the Master Dashboard and FactSet, as noted under each; drawn charts take their figures from the memo.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
